t: Nahuatl, a Uto-Aztecan language that came to central Mexico from the north, was the language of the Aztecs and the common language of trade and empire across much of Mesoamerica.

After the Spanish conquest it was written in the Latin alphabet, producing a large body of Indigenous writing, from chronicles, poetry and wills to the Florentine Codex, one of the greatest records of a society before European rule.
Still spoken by about 1.7 million people in Mexico, it has given words such as chocolate, tomato, avocado and chili to languages around the world.
dyk: Mexico takes its name from the Mexica, the Nahuatl-speaking founders of Tenochtitlan, and the name of Guatemala comes from a Nahuatl word meaning “place of many trees”.
ev: Tula, the city of the Toltecs, whose people probably spoke Nahuatl, dominates central Mexico
The Mexica found Tenochtitlan, by tradition, on an island in Lake Texcoco
Malintzin, a Nahuatl-speaking woman, becomes the interpreter of Hernán Cortés
The College of Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco opens, teaching Latin, Spanish and Nahuatl to young Nahua nobles
Alonso de Molina publishes his great dictionary of Nahuatl and Spanish
Bernardino de Sahagún and Nahua scholars complete the Florentine Codex
A royal decree of Charles III calls for Spanish to replace the Indigenous languages of the empire
Mexico’s law on linguistic rights recognises Nahuatl and other Indigenous languages as national languages

f.family: Uto-Aztecan: the Nahuan branch, related to languages of northern Mexico and the western United States such as Hopi, Comanche and Huichol
f.script: Aztec pictorial writing, with glyphs for names, places and dates; from the 16th century the Latin alphabet
f.earliest: Name and place glyphs in Aztec manuscripts and monuments of the 15th century; alphabetic texts from the mid-16th century
f.status: Spoken by about 1.7 million people, the most widely spoken Indigenous language of Mexico; a national language of Mexico since 2003
